steps.explanationAfterStep: The arrow starts at the π bond, the electrons, and ends between the middle carbon and the cation: the positive charge itself never moves along an arrow. Both forms are equal, so the charge is shared by the end carbons. A nucleophile can attack either end.

title: Allyl cation resonance
subtitle: A π bond moves next to the empty p orbital
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 7 (Delocalization and conjugation)

form-1.caption: allyl cation, one resonance form (Cl⁻ is a spectator)
hintTiers: The positive carbon has an empty p orbital. Which electrons are next to it?
The C=C π bond can slide over towards the positive carbon. One arrow.
One arrow: the C=C π bond into the bond between the middle carbon and the positive carbon.
form-1.learnerPrompt: Draw the other resonance form of the allyl cation. Move only π bonds.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Resonance arrows never break or make σ bonds: the atoms stay exactly where they are. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.
Putting the π pair on one carbon makes a carbanion next to positive carbons: more charges, not a shifted one. Move the π pair towards the empty p orbital instead.

form-2.caption: allyl cation, the other resonance form (Cl⁻ is a spectator)

mechanismSummary: The C=C π bond moves one place along the chain, towards the positive carbon. The positive charge moves to the other end: it is shared by the two end carbons and never sits on the middle one.
